title: The Forecast That Shows Its Work
concept: USGS posted odds for aftershocks twelve hours after the October 15th M5.6 near Lake Minchumina. The film makes the odds physical (a hundred tiles, a bin of a thousand grains), shows that the forecast gives a range, a count, its own weak spot and the time of its next update, lets the strongest fair objection stand (one quake can't grade a probability), and ends on what any forecast, human or machine, should show. A thermal slip printed by a seismic station is the throughline and the verdict stays pending.

fingerprint.palette: midnight teal, tungsten amber, chalk white, brass, one alarm vermilion, pre-dawn blue
fingerprint.light_story: 3 a.m. tungsten night warming to snow-blue dawn as the slip fills
fingerprint.metaphor: a receipt printed by the ground itself

palette: midnight teal, tungsten amber, chalk white, brass, one alarm vermilion, pre-dawn blue
divergence_note: 10-15 was pearl fog daylight with a cranberry Gate and 10-11 first-light rose tundra with a medicine crate. This film opens in a black-spruce night under one tungsten lamp on a round brass instrument with a face, moves through a clock void, a desk, a tile board, a dial panel, a pegboard and a map, and ends at a corkboard at dawn. The hero is an instrument that listens, the throughline is a paper receipt, and the palette is night teal, tungsten and chalk with no cranberry or pearl.

treatment.winner: The Dramatist's 3 a.m. frame and Slip, with the Explainer's hundred-tile board and bin, the Comedian's tape peel and the Enthusiast's ask-for-the-slip corkboard.
treatment.why: The Dramatist's night and its tape-peel loop carry the honest turn, the Explainer's tile counts make the odds felt, and the Enthusiast's button turns the point into something a viewer can ask for.

angle.thesis: The USGS forecast for the Lake Minchumina quake shows what a number worth leaning on looks like: odds instead of promises, a range, its own printed weak spot and the time of its next check.
supporting_facts: c5 to c8: the ladder from about 40 in 100 (M3+) down to under 1 in 1,000 (M6+) in one week
c14 and c13: a 95 percent range of 0 to 5, from a count of 1 at issue time
c15 and c16: it prints where it may perform poorly, and when it will check itself again
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: One quake can't grade a probability, and by USGS's own account the model may perform poorly when big aftershocks set off their own (c15), the Japan 2011 case (c17). The checklist proves a forecast CAN be checked, not that it is right. Accuracy is the next question.
angle.falsifiability: False if the printed update doesn't arrive, or the week's M3+ count lands outside 0 to 5 AND USGS gives no account of it, or if the posting rule is discretionary. Verdict pending, the film says the week isn't over.
angle.second_movement: Walk the ladder down so the viewer feels the reassurance hidden in the headline number, then turn: the weak spot printed on the page is the cascading case (Japan), the one where the stakes are highest.
angle.ai_point_OUR_READ: Labelled opinion. No claim the model is or isn't AI. Whatever tool makes a number for Alaskans, human or machine, this is the bar: odds, a range, its limits, the time it checks again.
angle.valence: Upbeat, a public-science win credited plainly, one earned counter-scene.

runner_up_angles.C: 3 a.m. human (merged, cold open and ladder)

angle.debate: A's pending-verdict honesty kept (no pass claimed). B's 'disclosure not math' defends against 'rewards the old method'. C's strongest counter (calm confident answer comforts more) is answered by the ladder itself holding real reassurance. Stance: celebratory with a curious turn.
